stories.topic: The Reformers Won the Argument Decades Before 1991
stories.summary: Amit asks how the 1991 reforms could have happened so fast without public consultation. Ajay rebuts the framing using customs duties: starting in the 1960s, Bhagwati, T.N. Srinivasan and Manmohan Singh's PhD thesis launched a generation-long argument among economists. Conference after conference, the 'lefties and nationalists' lost. By 1991, going from 350% duty to 5% wasn't a debate — only the sequencing was. The 'speed' of '91 was the public-debate stage being already complete.
stories.insight: Apparent overnight reforms are usually the visible peak of a 20-30 year underwater iceberg of data, research, and intellectual contestation. When the foundation is missing, the reforms that 'happen quickly' tend to fail — and that's also why they fail.

stories.topic: Turning Down Kirit Parikh at 21 — The Worst Decision He Ever Made
stories.summary: When Divyanshu asked Ajay on the spot to name a mistake, he reached for age 21. Just out of IIT, the great economist Kirit Parikh told him, 'You're a good child, come apprentice with me for some years.' Ajay turned him down — glamorised by the idea of doing a PhD in the United States. In hindsight he calls it 'the dumbest decision imaginable': he could have had four one-on-one sessions a week with Parikh — the greatest education in the world possible — and chose credentialism and US glamour instead.
stories.insight: Apprenticeship with a great mind beats credentials at a great institution. Credentialism is one of the most expensive mistakes a young, ambitious person makes — because the costs are invisible (the apprenticeship you didn't take) and the benefits are ego-shaped.

stories.topic: The Hunter-Gatherer Was Free; Agriculture Was a Catastrophe
stories.summary: The childhood story is wrong. The transition from hunter-gatherer to agricultural life was a brutal regression: disease appeared, male skeletons shrank from six feet (heights not regained until the 20th century), women were turned into property and socially regulated, grain enabled state formation, and early states existed only to tax and conscript. From the rise of agriculture in Babylon ~5000 years ago to the 19th-century emergence of liberal democracy, much of human history was a 'long dark regress.' If you could choose, you would always choose to be born a hunter-gatherer.
stories.insight: Linear-progress narratives are programming, not data. For most humans across most of history, the state was an enemy to flee from, not a service to receive — a frame that still describes how a great many Indians silently relate to their government.

stories.topic: The 20th Century As a Stress-Test for the Idea of Progress
stories.summary: Pick any 20-year-old or 60-year-old in the 20th century at random. For huge fractions of them, the rest of life went terribly: World Wars, Russian Revolution, Nazi Germany ('Nazi' is two bad ideas — nationalist and socialist — fused), the looming threat of nuclear war and communist expansion. The 1989 collapse of the USSR generated worldwide hope: 'this nightmare is ending, market economies and liberal democracy everywhere.' By 2024, that hope is largely betrayed. Russia became Putin, Hungary became 'one of the most disgusting countries,' Poland nearly went the same way, China went from Deng's reform to Xi's absolutism, and large-scale land warfare returned to Europe in 2022.
stories.insight: 'Social and political catastrophe is always possible' should be a guiding principle. Progress is a thing to strive for, not a thing to count on. The discipline this enforces — wariness, contingency planning, citizenship — is precisely what an unwarranted faith in progress destroys.

stories.topic: Tyrants Want People, Not Territory — So Run Away
stories.summary: Drawing on James C. Scott, Ajay reframes the state's deep history. Lines on maps are a silly modern idea; for most of human history, what tyrants actually wanted was bodies — more people to tax, conscript, and oppress. The rational response of pre-modern peoples was to run away into the hills, the forests, the swamps. Statelessness, even anarchy, was often preferable to life under a predatory state. This is, Ajay notes, 'more than a shadow' of how a vast portion of Indian society still relates to government — keep far, far away from it.
stories.insight: The state's modern self-image as servant of the people is a thin veneer over a much older identity as predator. When Indians distrust government instinctively, they're channelling thousands of years of wisdom — not failing to be modern.

stories.topic: Society Changes 10% At A Time — Through One Conversation
stories.summary: Ajay describes his own arc on persuasion. As a boy, he believed a clean argument from Newton's laws to Kepler's would shatter superstition instantly. Then for decades he descended into gloom: nobody actually persuades anybody, we just talk past each other on private random walks. Now, 'all grown up,' he believes a third position. In a zone of truth and trust, you'll never get the other person to admit they were wrong (human frailty), but they will quietly update by 10% over time. And 10% is a lot. If you persuade ten people by 10% on a couple of important things, that is the engine of social change.
stories.insight: Persuasion is invisible, delayed, partial, and ego-protected — and it works anyway. The mistake is expecting visible capitulation; the reality is a slow, unannounced 10% drift in private.

stories.topic: Bertolt Brecht's 'The Solution' — When the Government Dissolves the People
stories.summary: After the East German uprising of 17 June 1953, the Secretary of the Writers Union distributed leaflets saying the people had squandered the government's confidence and could only win it back by redoubled work. Brecht responded with the satirical poem: 'Would it not in that case be simpler / for the government / To dissolve the people / and elect another?' Amit reads it out as the canonical case of the state-people inversion — where the state, instead of serving the people, demands the people serve it.
stories.insight: Brecht's lethal joke is the operating logic of every illiberal regime in miniature. When you find yourself blaming 'the people' for failing the state's vision, you've already inverted the moral relationship between citizen and government.

stories.topic: How Amit Shifted His Own Overton Window of Podcast Length
stories.summary: Amit half-jokes that he personally shifted the Overton window of podcast duration in India. When he started, one hour was considered a 'deep dive.' By doing five-hour and six-hour episodes on The Seen and the Unseen, he made two-hour and three-hour conversations feel normal. Now a one-hour podcast is 'a mini.'
stories.insight: An Overton window doesn't move on its own — somebody has to plant a flag at what currently seems an extreme and live there long enough that the centre of gravity drags toward them. Even formats and forms have Overton windows.

stories.topic: The Joint Secretaries Watching In Protest
stories.summary: Mid-explanation of his policy pipeline, Ajay says drily 'in a good country, elected legislators write laws; in a bad country, the joint secretary writes the law' — and that joint secretaries 'don't know much.' Amit cuts in: at this very moment, this episode is being played on a giant screen in a hall full of joint secretaries gathering to protest everything Ajay has said about them. 'You of all people with a broken ankle, you don't even have all your joints.'
stories.insight: A perfect example of EIE's running self-parody: even as Ajay makes a serious institutional point, Amit deflates the moment with a visualised counterfactual of bureaucratic outrage. The wit is the leavening; the point survives intact.

recommendations.item: Weapons of the Weak
recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's study of subtle, everyday forms of resistance — foot-dragging, false compliance, pilfering, feigned ignorance — by subordinate groups against predatory states.
recommendations.reason: The companion piece to Against the Grain. If states emerged to tax and conscript, large numbers of people throughout history just wanted the state to leave them alone — and they had ingenious quiet methods of doing so. Ajay sees 'more than a shadow' of this disposition in much of Indian society today.

recommendations.item: Runaway
recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: A short-story collection by Amit's favourite living writer, the Canadian Nobel laureate.
recommendations.reason: Munro sets her stories in one province of Canada but captures the human condition with such depth that she is beloved everywhere — proof that good fiction is universal. A deliberate counterweight to an episode about states and policy.

recommendations.item: Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage
recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: Another Munro short-story masterpiece.
recommendations.reason: Recommended together with Runaway as the two collections to start with for anyone discovering Munro.

recommendations.item: The Bear Came Over the Mountain
recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: A specific Munro short story, originally published in The New Yorker and freely readable online.
recommendations.reason: Possibly Amit's favourite short story of all time. 'Just magnificent.' A specific entry point into Munro for anyone unsure where to begin.

recommendations.item: The Solution
recommendations.creator: Bertolt Brecht
recommendations.context: Brecht's brief satirical poem written after the 1953 East German workers' uprising.
recommendations.reason: The canonical literary statement of state-people inversion. Read it out in episode as the foundational text for thinking about regimes that blame the people for failing them.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE episode on the people who fought decades-long battles for India's economic reforms.
recommendations.reason: The proximate cause of this episode. Amit was left, at the end of it, asking the larger question: what motivates people to play such long games against the tide?

recommendations.item: The Ideas of Our Constitution (Episode 164 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Madhav Khosla)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Madhav Khosla
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Madhav Khosla on India's constitutional founding.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Khosla articulates the 'pedagogic' and 'transformative' framing of the Indian constitution — the top-down theory of change that Amit pushes back against here.

recommendations.item: Mera Joota Hai Japani
recommendations.creator: Shailendra (lyrics), Shankar-Jaikishan (music), from Raj Kapoor's Shree 420
recommendations.context: The famous 1955 Bollywood song: 'My shoes are Japanese, my trousers English, my red cap Russian — but my heart is still Indian.'
recommendations.reason: Amit cues it as the anthem of globalization's cultural reality — that hybridity is the real condition of identity, and that monolithic 'pure' nationalism collides with how people actually live.

recommendations.item: The End of History?
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Fukuyama's famous 1989 essay (note the question mark) declaring the post-Soviet triumph of liberal democracy.
recommendations.reason: The classic statement of the progress-is-inevitable view that 1989 seemed to vindicate — and that the 21st century has spectacularly falsified, lending weight to Ajay's warning that catastrophe is always possible.

recommendations.item: Against the Grain
recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's revisionist deep history of how grain-based agriculture enabled the rise of the early state.
recommendations.reason: The companion to Weapons of the Weak. Source of Ajay's argument that the agricultural revolution was a regression for ordinary people — disease, social control, women as property, taxation, and conscription. The 'long dark' from Babylon to the 19th century.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's earlier episode on the 2022 return of large-scale land war in Europe.
recommendations.reason: The detailed back-up to Ajay's point that the 21st century has produced the kind of war Europeans thought ended in 1945 — a vivid demonstration that political catastrophe is never closed off.

recommendations.item: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Ajay and Renuka Sane on Indian pension reform.
recommendations.reason: Concrete example of Ajay's policy pipeline at work — a multi-decade journey from data to research to imaginative solutions to public debate to law and organisation design.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Amit's exhaustive episode with the bureaucrat-reformer KP Krishnan.
recommendations.reason: A living portrait of the policy pipeline. Ajay points to Krishnan's circle as people who 'over a period of time' actually built the institutions Indians benefit from today.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's foundational episode on the nature of the state.
recommendations.reason: Background reading for anyone who wants the pre-history of the policy pipeline laid out here.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on market failure and when state intervention is justified.
recommendations.reason: Specifically referenced as the place to elaborate on stage three of the policy pipeline — identifying market failures and imagining low-coercion solutions.

recommendations.item: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Episode 27 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode connecting vaccines, freedom, and the limits of state coercion.
recommendations.reason: The third in EIE's trilogy on the nature of the state — recommended as further reading on what the state should and should not do.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's primer on public choice theory — politicians and bureaucrats as self-interested actors.
recommendations.reason: Linked from the show notes as part of the broader EIE corpus on how state behaviour actually works, beyond the textbook view.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the failures of universities, research, and India's knowledge ecosystem.
recommendations.reason: Cited in this episode for Ajay's complaint that the formal academy in India does not do the imaginative-policy-solution stage of the pipeline — covered in detail there.

recommendations.item: But clouds got in my way: Bias and bias-correction of VIIRS nighttime lights data in the presence of clouds
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: An XKDR Forum paper on improving NASA's methodology for processing nighttime lights data to measure prosperity at half-kilometre resolution.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's example of being at the global frontier on satellite-derived data — proof that 'the bird in the sky sees the damn truth' and that India can build measurement systems independent of an uncooperative ISRO.

recommendations.item: Kashi Ka Assi
recommendations.creator: Kashinath Singh
recommendations.context: A Hindi novel set in Banaras.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's quoted line, 'Bharme Jaye Duniya, Hum Bajayein Harmonia' — the world goes to hell, I'll play my harmonium. The temptation Ajay has to argue against in the second half of the episode.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah on state capacity, governance and institutions (Episode 18 of Jack of All Knowledge)
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah on Jack of All Knowledge
recommendations.context: An interview where Divyanshu asked Ajay on the spot to name a mistake.
recommendations.reason: The episode where the host's surprise question elicited Ajay's confession about turning down Kirit Parikh's apprenticeship offer — the seed of this episode's most personal anecdote.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's policy book.
recommendations.reason: Linked from the show notes; the deeper textbook treatment of the policy pipeline Ajay walks through here from data to research to implementation.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's online writing course.
recommendations.reason: Standard cross-promotion in EIE show notes for listeners who want to write better — itself an exercise in the long, slow accretion of skill the episode endorses.

core_ideas.concept: The Policy Pipeline (Left to Right, No Skipping Steps)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's flagship framework for how the state actually changes. Stage 1: Data — without measurement you are vulnerable to spectacle and the loudest megaphone wins. Stage 2: Research — refining raw data into knowledge, both correlations and causation. Stage 3: Imaginative policy solutions — identifying genuine market failures and inventing the lowest-coercion ways to address them. Stage 4: Vibrant public debate — many rival ideas argued in good faith, requiring freedom of speech. Stage 5: Government expert committees — wise people with one foot in intellect and one in establishment, sifting and legitimising ideas. Stage 6: Decision and implementation — drafting laws (in a good country, by elected legislators; in a bad country, by joint secretaries) and designing the organisation that will execute them. The pipeline takes about 25 years. There is no shortcut.
core_ideas.quote: Does it take 25 years? Yes. But there is no other way.

core_ideas.concept: State vs People vs The Random Bloke Who Won A Match
core_ideas.explanation: Indians habitually conflate three different things: the state, the people, and any individual who briefly does something visible. 'India won the World Cup' is silly — some guys won, neither the people nor the state had anything to do with it. Once you separate them properly, you realise that most of what is good (truth, beauty, creativity, wealth) lives in the people, and most of the rot too — the crushing of freedom, the casual cruelties — also lies in the social. Defaulting to 'sarkar will fix it' is the deepest Indian intellectual error. We are too statist; we should be more interested in what people can do for each other.
core_ideas.quote: Some bloke won some sports match. There is the people of India and there is the state. It's good to separate them.

core_ideas.concept: Progress Is Not Inevitable — The 20th Century As Counter-Example
core_ideas.explanation: The Enlightenment-era assumption that history bends toward justice and freedom is not a scientific claim — the sample size is tiny. The 20th century stress-tested the idea: World Wars, Russian Revolution, Nazi rule, the Cold War. Even the 1989 hope of post-Soviet liberal democracy has largely collapsed by 2024 — democratic backsliding is the rule, not the exception. So the discipline is: dream of progress, work for it, but never take it for granted. 'Social and political catastrophe is always possible' should be a guiding principle. Ajay tells the gentle reader: imagine standing in 1918 Weimar; imagine standing in 1989 Russia. Things can go very, very wrong.
core_ideas.quote: Social and political catastrophe is always possible.

core_ideas.concept: Agriculture As Regression (and States As Predators of Bodies)
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on James C. Scott. The childhood story — hunter-gatherer to agriculture is progress — is wrong. Agriculture brought disease, height shrinkage, women becoming property, and the rise of states whose business was taxation and conscription. Tyrants didn't really want territory; they wanted bodies to control. Pre-modern people frequently fled to escape state grasp; statelessness was often preferable. The 'long dark' from Babylon ~5000 years ago to the 19th-century rise of liberal democracy is mostly regression for ordinary people. This deep history still informs how Indians instinctively relate to their state.
core_ideas.quote: It is better to live in a state of anarchy where there is no state than to live with a tyrannical state.

core_ideas.concept: The Demand and Supply Side of the Political Marketplace
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's earlier framing was that real change comes from changing the people — the demand side — because supply (the state) responds to demand. He has since refined this. Even small incremental supply-side changes from inside the policy world matter, and the two are complementary, not competitive. You need the citizen screaming around restrictions, and you need the elite project of diagnosis and prescription. Globalization in India was almost purely an elite project (because anti-foreigner sentiment is the easy populist default), while gay-marriage legalisation across the world was almost purely a popular-opinion project that the state followed.
core_ideas.quote: It is very easy for a feeble mind to slip into anti-foreigner.

core_ideas.concept: Global Examples of Theory of Change — Two Templates
core_ideas.explanation: Two illuminating templates from the late 20th and early 21st century. Template 1 (people-led): worldwide movement for decriminalisation of homosexuality and gay marriage — opinion shifted in the public, the state followed in country after country. Template 2 (elite-led): India's 1991 trade liberalisation — populist instinct was anti-foreigner, but a small intellectual community (Bhagwati, Srinivasan, Manmohan Singh, Vajpayee, Rao, Chidambaram, Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Narasimha Rao) had won the argument among themselves over 30 years and translated it into reality when the autarchic system stalled. Different problems demand different routes.

core_ideas.concept: Fame Is A Curse (And Why Common Knowledge Is Wrong)
core_ideas.explanation: An aside that doubles as an epistemic principle. In almost any field, when you actually get the microscope going, what is loudly stated by all the famous people turns out to be wrong. Fame interferes with information, because it rewards the loud, the simple, and the spectacle-friendly. A working society needs many ways of measurement and analysis that are immune to the megaphone — including, increasingly, satellite imagery, which 'sees the damn truth' regardless of who is loud on the ground.
core_ideas.quote: Fame is a curse — it interferes with information.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing of state action: every law, every tax, every regulation is ultimately backed by coercion. Even tax money is 'made out of coercion.' So the right design question is always: what is the lowest-coercion way of substantively getting the job done — even if that means only 60% of the job, not 100%? The temptation to reach for big regulatory hammers (e.g., regulating tech giants) ignores that you are arming the worst future occupant of that office. Imagine the worst person you can think of with that power.
core_ideas.quote: The poison that the state drips on the people is coercion.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's mature theory of persuasion. Lectures don't change minds in real time — and people are too proud to admit they were wrong. But in a zone of trust, a good conversation will produce a quiet 10% shift in the listener over weeks or months. They will never tell you. But it happens. Persuade ten people by 10% on a couple of important things and you have meaningfully changed the world. Mass-megaphone advocacy on social media achieves precisely nothing; eye-contact conversations carry the actual weight.
core_ideas.quote: We will never shift our views by 100%, but we shift by 10%. And 10% is a lot.

core_ideas.explanation: If progress is not inevitable, the Indian elite reformer can't fuel themselves on triumphalism or speed. The wrong theory of change burns people out fast — they bang their head against a 'mad bugger's wall' and break. The right disposition is paced, transactional-zero, dharma-driven: do the work because it is your responsibility, not because you expect a reward. Don't ask the world for credit. Don't demand outcomes. Find emotional stamina. The single highest superpower is the ability to keep going.
core_ideas.quote: Don't ask for anything, don't ask for a reward, don't ask for success.

core_ideas.concept: The Western Way of War — Honest Post-Mortems In Community
core_ideas.explanation: A discipline India lacks. After every campaign, write the war diaries; celebrate successes; excoriate failures; cry together about what went wrong; debate dispassionately. Practise telling each other the truth ('You have to be the person who tells me I'm full of shit'). The opposite — childish triumphalism on one side, collapse-and-blame on the other — is the Indian default and the reason institutional learning doesn't compound. Real communities of practice are built on honest failure analysis, and India's elite is still at the early stages of even understanding the word 'community.'

Ajay's introspection technique. Imagine you have a time machine and can write one letter to yourself at age X. What would you say? It works because the ego's default move is to write the past as a story of correctness ('I did everything right; the world did wrong'). The hypothetical letter forces you to actually identify mistakes — and the moment you can list 16 things you would have done differently, you have stepped onto the engine of knowledge. Doing this in community — with the people whose criticism you trust — compounds the learning.

core_ideas.concept: The Indian Constitution As 'Topsoil' On Illiberal Soil
core_ideas.explanation: Amit invokes Ambedkar's own framing — the constitution is only 'topsoil,' a thin liberal layer on a deeply illiberal society, designed to keep the society in check. Madhav Khosla's later framing of the constitution as 'pedagogic' or 'transformative' assumes the same top-down theory. Amit's critique: this assumption was wrong. Real change does not flow from constitution to people; it must come from within society. Many of those who would otherwise have built the better society stopped trying once independence was won, trusting the document to do the work. It hasn't.

core_ideas.concept: The Overton Window As A Strategic Object
core_ideas.explanation: Defined by Amit for the gentle reader: the range of positions currently considered 'within' acceptable public discourse. The work of long-game change is to widen the window — to make ideas that were unthinkable thirty years ago (e.g., gay marriage) feel normal, then mainstream, then so settled there is no debate. Government expert committees historically did this in India — they read public debate and legitimised heretical ideas by including them in consensus reports. Amit cheekily claims credit for shifting the Overton window of podcast duration in India.

core_ideas.concept: The Dialectic Wants You Even If You Don't Want It
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's response to the Kashi-Ka-Assi cynic — 'the world is going to hell; I will play my harmonium.' The pure self-interest argument: you have skin in the game whether you like it or not. If you were a 1933 German, your number-one job was understanding politics so you could leave in time. Even with zero altruism, the efficient thing is to study the world, form a theory, stay engaged. Otherwise, you are 'a little breadcrumb' that society and state will chew over without noticing.
core_ideas.quote: You may not be interested in the dialectic, but the dialectic is interested in you.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens by demanding coffee mid-introduction: 'Wait. Need coffee.' That was quick.

Amit's running gag about the gross national product of EIE: 'I have a useful correlation with a fantastic insight — the total hours watched of Everything Is Everything has been going up at the same time that India's GDP is going up. So the prosperity of our nation relies upon us.'
Amit's commission-economy jab: governments can 'set up a commission to compose a sonata, set up a commission to come up with a new raga which is nationalistic.'

Amit's flippant defence of bad news: 'In a sense it is good that we are not progressing but going backwards and we are surrounded by bad news everywhere — because the creator economy is booming and Ajay Shah, we need content.' Ajay's reply: 'Yeah. Like if there had been no war in Ukraine, what episode would you make?'

Amit on Ajay's broken ankle and the joint secretaries: 'At this moment in time, this very episode is being played on a giant screen in a large hall full of joint secretaries who have gathered to protest against everything that you are saying about them. There's nothing wrong with joint secretaries. And you of all people with a broken ankle, you don't even have all your joints.'
Amit on the 10% theory: 'You know, right after this recording I am going to ask you for 10 Diet Cokes. So you change your views by ten percent and give me one.'
Ajay's drily devastating definition of Nazism: 'Nazi stands for nationalist socialist. It's like the two bad ideas fused into one.'
Amit asks what 'dialectic' means in 'simple English, mango logon ke liye.'
Ajay's self-deprecation about persuasion: 'I am a stupid monkey walking on the prairie and I have the inability to say that I was wrong.'

Bertolt Brecht's poem 'The Solution': 'Would it not in that case be simpler / for the government / To dissolve the people / and elect another?' — read out by Amit as the canonical satire of state-people inversion.
Mera joota hai Japani, yeh patloon Englistani / Sar pe lal topi Roosi, phir bhi dil hai Hindustani — the Shree 420 song cued up as the anthem of identity-as-hybridity.
Bhar mein jaye duniya, hum bajayein harmonia — from Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi. The world is going to hell; I will play my harmonium. Used as the cynic's slogan that Ajay must answer.
Tagore quoted via Amit's beloved Robi-Da: 'Jodi Tor Daak Shune Keu Na Aashe, Tobe Ekla Cholo Re' — if no one heeds your call, walk alone.
Martin Luther King: 'The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice' — invoked and then questioned by Amit.
Max Planck (paraphrased): 'Paradigms change one funeral at a time' — invoked as the slow generational mechanism of intellectual change.
Alexander Pope's Newton epitaph: 'Nature and Nature's Laws lay hid in night: God said, Let Newton be! and all was light.' Ajay's gloss on the magical opening of the scientific revolution.
Thomas Jefferson: 'The price of liberty is eternal vigilance' — Amit's rejoinder to Ajay's warning about catastrophe.
Margaret Thatcher (paraphrased): you have to fight some battles again and again, you can't win them once.
Benjamin Franklin's reply at the U.S. Constitutional Convention: 'A republic — if you can keep it.' Ajay can't recall the speaker by name; that's the figure.
Gandhi: 'Be the change that you want to see in the world' — invoked twice as the unit-of-action principle.

Albert Einstein (Amit's quiz answer): 'It's not that I'm so smart, it's just that I stay with problems longer.' Plus the legend that at 16 Einstein imagined riding a beam of light and stayed with the question for years until special relativity arrived.
Confucius: 'It does not matter how slowly you go, as long as you do not stop.'
Vivian Greene: 'Don't wait for the storms to pass, learn to dance in the rain.'
Stephen Pinker's 'better angels of our nature' invoked as the optimistic side of human hardwiring that culture is meant to amplify.
Yes Minister — referenced as the source of the joke: 'Something must be done. X is something. Therefore X must be done.'
Robi-Da (Rabindranath Tagore): 'Shob kichu, shob kichu' — everything is everything — invoked as the unifying refrain of the show, the great Bengali poet co-opted as patron saint.
